section_1.title: The Paradox of Instantaneous Motion
section_1.content: Introduce the fundamental problem: How can we measure speed at a single, static point in time? Use the concept of 'Average vs. Instantaneous' velocity to motivate the need for calculus.
section_1.example: A cheetah chasing a gazelle: If the cheetah's speed is changing constantly, the speedometer shows a different number every millisecond.

section_2.title: The Method of Exhaustion (Limits)
section_2.content: Explain the concept of a 'Limit'. Visualize a curve being approximated by shorter and shorter straight line segments. As the segments become infinitely small, the approximation converges to the curve itself.
section_2.example: An animation of a polygon inside a circle; as the number of sides increases, the polygon's perimeter and area 'melt' into the shape of the circle.

section_3.title: The Derivative: Seeing the Slope
section_3.content: Define the derivative as the 'rate of change' at a single point (the slope of the tangent line). Visually demonstrate the 'zoom-in' effect where a complex curve looks like a straight line at an microscopic level.
section_3.example: A mountain climber's path: The derivative represents the exact steepness of the terrain under their feet at any specific second.

section_4.title: The Integral: Accumulating the Whole
section_4.content: Define the integral as the reverse of the derivative—summing up an infinite number of tiny slices to find a total. Connect this to finding the area under a curve.
section_4.example: A robotic arm painting a curved wall: The integral calculates the total amount of paint used by summing up millions of tiny, thin vertical strips of paint.

section_5.title: The Fundamental Theorem: The Bridge
section_5.content: Conclude by showing how the derivative (splitting apart) and the integral (putting together) are inverse operations, linking the two seemingly different concepts into one powerful framework.
section_5.example: A digital music player: The sound wave is stored as a collection of instantaneous points (derivative-like), and the player 'integrates' them to reconstruct the continuous melody you hear.
